\title{Distribution-Preserving QIM: Trading Noise Margin for Statistical
Undetectability and Scaling Robustness in Invisible Watermarking}

\author{\IEEEauthorblockN{Abhishek Sairam Gaduputi}
\IEEEauthorblockA{Department of Data Science\\
New Jersey Institute of Technology\\
Newark, NJ 07102, USA\\
ag2936@njit.edu}}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Quantization index modulation (QIM) watermarks write DCT coefficients onto a
lattice, leaving a discrete histogram fingerprint of the kind that black-box
removal attacks such as UnMarker search for. We study
\emph{Distribution-Preserving QIM} (DP-QIM), which partitions the natural
distribution of a DCT coefficient into equal-mass cells and, when a coefficient
must change cells to carry its bit, replaces it with a natural sample from the
target cell. We compare DP-QIM with classical QIM at the same DCT position and
matched PSNR on 44 crops from 15 real photographs, using source-grouped
cross-validation and bootstrap confidence intervals. DP-QIM is close to
undetectable: a learned histogram detector reaches ROC-AUC
$0.52\,[0.49,0.57]$ against DP-QIM versus $0.90\,[0.78,1.00]$ against QIM at
64~bits, and $0.61$ versus $1.00$ at 256~bits, while the UnMarker peak
statistic stays at chance. Because one-bit DP-QIM cells split at the
coefficient median, which is exactly zero for the AC coefficient we use, decoding is a
sign test that is invariant to amplitude scaling, giving $+35$~pp bit accuracy
under Gaussian blur, $+34$~pp under $0.5\times$ downscaling and $+20$~pp under
$0.5\times$ contrast scaling. The price is noise margin: QIM is more robust to
JPEG ($Q{=}90$: $-15$~pp; $Q{=}70$: $-28$~pp) and additive noise ($-14$~pp), and
an UnMarker-style removal attack degrades DP-QIM 3 to 7~pp more than QIM.
Statistical undetectability alone therefore does not confer removal
resistance. Code and the full evaluation protocol are
released.\footnote{\url{https://github.com/sairam782/Invisible-Watermarking}}
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
invisible watermarking, quantization index modulation, DCT, steganalysis,
valumetric scaling, AI-generated content provenance
\end{IEEEkeywords}

%------------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

Invisible watermarks are a primary tool for tracing the provenance of images,
including AI-generated ones~\cite{Cox2007book}. Recent work shows they are
fragile against adaptive adversaries. UnMarker~\cite{Kassis2025unmarker}
removes deployed watermarks without access to the detector or the key by
locating spectral regions whose statistics differ from those of natural images
and perturbing them, and regeneration attacks remove watermarks by re-synthesizing
the image~\cite{Zhao2023removable,Erasing2024neurips}.

Quantization index modulation (QIM)~\cite{Chen2001qim} and its descendants are
especially exposed to the first kind of attack. QIM writes each carrier
coefficient onto one of two interleaved lattices, so the marginal histogram of
watermarked coefficients collapses onto isolated spikes
(Fig.~\ref{fig:hist}, middle), a fingerprint natural images do not have.
This paper asks a narrow question: \emph{if a QIM-style watermark is
constrained to leave the coefficient marginal natural, what does it gain and
what does it lose?}

We study Distribution-Preserving QIM (DP-QIM). It partitions the empirical
distribution of a coefficient into $2M$ equal-mass cells with alternating bit
labels; a coefficient already in a cell carrying its bit is left unchanged,
and otherwise it is replaced by a natural sample drawn from the interior of an
adjacent cell. Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}
\item The DP-QIM embedding rule and two properties: the watermarked marginal
is a two-component mixture of natural distributions (Prop.~\ref{prop:ks}), and
one-bit DP-QIM decoding is invariant to amplitude scaling, whereas lattice
decoding is not (Prop.~\ref{prop:scale}).
\item A leakage-free comparison protocol for quantization watermarks: both
methods at the same DCT position, robustness curves compared at matched PSNR,
cross-validation grouped by source photograph, an attacker whose statistics
are independent of the embedder's, and bootstrap confidence intervals
(Sec.~\ref{sec:protocol}).
\item An empirical characterization of the trade-off on real photographs:
near-chance detectability and large gains under scaling-type attacks, paid for
with reduced margin against requantization and additive noise
(Sec.~\ref{sec:results}).
\end{enumerate}

\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.92\textwidth]{figures/fig1_histograms_v2.pdf}
\caption{Histogram (log scale) of DCT coefficient $(3,3)$ over every block of

%------------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related}

\textbf{QIM and its variants.} QIM~\cite{Chen2001qim} and dither modulation
are provably good under additive noise~\cite{PerezGonzalez2003knownhost} but
fragile to valumetric (amplitude) scaling. Rational dither
modulation~\cite{PerezGonzalez2005rdm}, angle QIM~\cite{Ourique2005angleqim}
and perceptually scaled QIM~\cite{Li2007perceptualqim} restore scaling
robustness by making the quantizer gain-adaptive. These schemes still write onto
a (scaled) lattice; DP-QIM instead obtains scaling invariance as a by-product
of matching the natural marginal, and our contribution is the joint behaviour
of undetectability and robustness rather than scaling robustness per se. We
do not compare against these gain-invariant variants
(Sec.~\ref{sec:limitations}).

\textbf{Learned watermarks.} HiDDeN~\cite{Zhu2018hidden},
StegaStamp~\cite{Tancik2020stegastamp}, Stable
Signature~\cite{Fernandez2023stablesignature} and
InvisMark~\cite{Xu2025invismark} train encoder-decoder networks against
differentiable distortion layers. They are robust to common processing but
remain vulnerable to regeneration~\cite{Zhao2023removable} and to
UnMarker~\cite{Kassis2025unmarker}. Analogous statistical-signature concerns
arise for language-model watermarks~\cite{Kirchenbauer2023llmwatermark}.

\textbf{Steganalysis and distribution preservation.} Steganography seeks to
hide the \emph{existence} of a message from statistical
detectors~\cite{Fridrich2009stegobook,Fridrich2012richmodels}, and
distribution-preserving embedding is a classical tool there. We borrow that
goal for robust watermarking, where the adversary's aim is removal rather than
detection, and measure undetectability with steganalysis-style detectors.

%------------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Distribution-Preserving QIM}
\label{sec:method}

\subsection{Setting}
An RGB image is converted to YCbCr (BT.601) and the luminance is split into
$8{\times}8$ blocks with orthonormal 2-D DCT. A payload of $P$ bits is carried
by one coefficient position $(u,v)$ in $P$ blocks chosen by a keyed
permutation over interior blocks (blocks touching reflect-padding are excluded
because padding is re-derived from modified pixels at decode time). Both
methods below use the same position and the same block selection.

\textbf{DCT-QIM baseline.} Dither-modulation QIM~\cite{Chen2001qim} with step
$\Delta$ snaps the carrier $c$ to $L_b = \{k\Delta + b\Delta/2\}$ and decodes
by the nearer of $L_0, L_1$.

\subsection{Embedding rule}
Let $F$ be the empirical CDF of coefficient $(u,v)$ over a training set of
natural images. For $M\geq1$, quantile boundaries
$F^{-1}(i/2M)$, $i=0,\dots,2M$, define cells $\mathcal{C}_0,\dots,\mathcal{C}_{2M-1}$
of equal natural mass with labels $\ell_i = i \bmod 2$. For a safety margin
$\epsilon>0$, the \emph{safe pool} $\mathcal{P}_i$ holds training coefficients
that lie in $\mathcal{C}_i$ at least $\epsilon$ from its finite boundaries.
To embed bit $b$ in a carrier $c$ with cell index $k$:
\begin{enumerate}
\item if $\ell_k = b$, leave $c$ unchanged;
\item otherwise, draw one keyed sample from each adjacent pool
$\mathcal{P}_{k\pm1}$ and replace $c$ with the one closer to $c$.
\end{enumerate}
The decoder returns the label of the cell containing the received
coefficient. All experiments use $M=1$; larger $M$ produced narrow cells near
the mode that did not survive 8-bit rounding.

\subsection{Properties}

\begin{proposition}[marginal]
\label{prop:ks}
Let $M=1$, payload bits be i.i.d.\ uniform, and $F_\epsilon$ be the natural
distribution conditioned on lying at least $\epsilon$ from the cell boundary.
Then the watermarked carrier distribution is
$P_W = \tfrac12 F + \tfrac12 F_\epsilon$, and
$\mathrm{KS}(P_W,F) = \tfrac12\,\mathrm{KS}(F_\epsilon,F) \to 0$ as
$\epsilon\to 0$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}[Sketch]
Each cell carries mass $\tfrac12$ and each bit matches the current label with
probability $\tfrac12$; matched carriers are untouched (distributed as $F$) and
the rest are drawn from the target cell's safe pool, which over both cells is
$F_\epsilon$. KS is linear in a mixture weight against a common component.
\end{proof}

By contrast, QIM's carrier distribution is supported on a lattice, so its KS
distance to $F$ is bounded away from zero for any $\Delta$.

\begin{proposition}[scaling]
\label{prop:scale}
Let an attack map the carrier $c \mapsto s\,c$ for some $s>0$.
(i) If the $M{=}1$ cell boundary is $0$, the DP-QIM decision $\mathbb{1}\{c>0\}$
is unchanged for every $s>0$.
(ii) A QIM carrier embedded at lattice value $c$ decodes correctly after
scaling iff $|1-s|\,|c| < \Delta/4$; for $s\le\tfrac12$ every carrier with
$|c|\ge\Delta/2$ lands on or beyond the decision boundary.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}[Sketch]
(i) $\operatorname{sign}(sc)=\operatorname{sign}(c)$. (ii) $L_0\cup L_1$ has
spacing $\Delta/2$, so decoding is correct iff the carrier moves by less than
$\Delta/4$; the move is $|1-s||c|$.
\end{proof}

The natural median of coefficient $(3,3)$ over our data is exactly $0$, so (i)
applies. Linear low-pass operations act approximately as per-coefficient
scaling: a Gaussian blur of standard deviation $\sigma$ attenuates frequency $f$
by $e^{-2\pi^2\sigma^2 f^2}$, which is $0.50$ at the $(3,3)$ basis frequency
($f{=}3/16$ cycles/pixel, $\sigma{=}1$) and $0.74$ at $(2,2)$. Prop.~\ref{prop:scale}
predicts that DP-QIM should gain most where attacks scale strongly, which is
what we observe (Sec.~\ref{sec:ablation}).

%------------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Evaluation Protocol}
\label{sec:protocol}

\textbf{Data.} We use the real photographs distributed with scikit-image and
Matplotlib (outdoor and indoor scenes, a portrait, natural textures, and
astronomical and microscopy images; synthetic and text images excluded): 15
sources, cut into 44 non-overlapping $256{\times}256$ crops (at most four per
source).

\textbf{Splits.} Five folds are grouped by \emph{source}, so no test crop
shares a photograph with any training crop. DP-QIM's CDF and pools, and the
attacker's natural reference, are fitted on training sources only. Every crop
is tested exactly once.

\textbf{Matched fidelity.} Both methods embed $P{=}64$ bits at the same
position (main results at $(3,3)$). We sweep DP-QIM's margin
$\epsilon\in\{0.5,1,2,3,4,6\}$ and QIM's step
$\Delta\in\{6,\dots,128\}$ (15 values spanning 46 to 72~dB), and compare
DP-QIM against the QIM curve linearly interpolated to DP-QIM's mean PSNR. We
never extrapolate beyond the sweep. Our main operating point is $\epsilon{=}2$
(53.9~dB), the smallest margin that decodes without attack (accuracy 0.999;
$\epsilon{=}0.5$ and $1$ give 0.949 and 0.976).

\textbf{Attacks.} JPEG ($Q{=}90,70$), additive Gaussian noise ($\sigma{=}0.03$
of full range), Gaussian blur ($\sigma{=}1$), $0.5\times$ bicubic
down-and-up-scaling, and contrast scaling about the image mean by $0.5$ and
$0.8$ (pure valumetric scaling of all AC coefficients).

\textbf{UnMarker-style removal.} We reimplement the attack's mechanism from
its description~\cite{Kassis2025unmarker}: for each of the 63 AC positions the
attacker compares the received image's coefficient histogram with a natural
reference built from \emph{training-source} images, flags bins whose density
exceeds the reference by a ratio $\tau$, and adds Gaussian jitter of $j$ times
the reference inter-quartile range to coefficients in flagged bins. The
attacker never sees the embedder's pools or key. Attack strength is identical
on both methods (attacked-image PSNR 47.0~dB for $\tau{=}2,j{=}0.5$ and
35.7~dB for $\tau{=}1.5,j{=}1$).

\textbf{Detectors.} (a) A learned detector: logistic regression on the
1-unit-bin histogram of the carrier position over \emph{all} blocks of an
image. Following Kerckhoffs' principle it knows the method and position, but
not the key, so it cannot isolate carrier blocks. (b) The unsupervised UnMarker
statistic: the maximum over-density of the image's histogram relative to a
reference built from other sources. Both are scored by ROC-AUC under
source-grouped five-fold evaluation, at $P\in\{64,256,1024\}$ (1024 = every
block), with QIM's $\Delta$ chosen to match DP-QIM's PSNR at each payload.

\textbf{Statistics.} All 95\% confidence intervals resample whole source
photographs (2{,}000 bootstrap replicates). Payload bits are seeded by CRC32
of the crop name, so every run is reproducible.

%------------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}

\subsection{Detectability}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Detector ROC-AUC with 95\% source-bootstrap CI (0.5 = chance).
DP-QIM $\epsilon{=}2$ against QIM at matched PSNR, position $(3,3)$.}
\label{tab:detect}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{\input{tables/detect.tex}}
\end{table}

Table~\ref{tab:detect} reports detectability. Against QIM, the learned
detector is near-perfect from 256~bits on, and already reaches 0.90 at 64~bits
even though only 6\% of blocks carry payload. Against DP-QIM it is at or near
chance at 64 and 256~bits, and its confidence intervals do not overlap QIM's.
The UnMarker peak statistic, which is the cue a statistical removal attack
relies on, is at chance for DP-QIM at 64 and 256~bits and rises only to
0.59 at full density, against 0.72 to 0.99 for QIM. At full density the learned
detector does gain some purchase on DP-QIM (0.77), consistent with
Prop.~\ref{prop:ks}: the safe-interior pool removes mass near the cell
boundary, a deficit that becomes measurable when every block is rewritten.

\subsection{Robustness at matched fidelity}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Bit accuracy of DP-QIM ($\epsilon{=}2$, 53.9~dB, position $(3,3)$,
64~bits) and its difference from PSNR-matched QIM. Bold: 95\% CI excludes
zero.}
\label{tab:robust}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{\input{tables/robustness.tex}}
\end{table}

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.92\textwidth]{figures/fig2_curves_v2.pdf}
\caption{Bit accuracy after attack versus PSNR of the watermarked image
(44 real crops, position $(3,3)$, 64~bits). QIM is a curve over its step
$\Delta$; DP-QIM points are its margin sweep. DP-QIM dominates under
scaling-type attacks (top row) and is dominated under requantization and
additive noise (bottom row).}
\label{fig:curves}
\end{figure*}

Table~\ref{tab:robust} and Fig.~\ref{fig:curves} show a clear split. Under
attacks that scale the carrier (Gaussian blur, downscaling and strong
contrast reduction), DP-QIM retains 0.83 to 0.97 accuracy while matched QIM is
near chance, a gain of $+20$ to $+35$~pp. Mild contrast scaling ($\times0.8$)
moves QIM carriers by less than $\Delta/4$ and leaves both methods intact, as
Prop.~\ref{prop:scale}(ii) predicts. Under JPEG and additive noise the
ordering reverses ($-14$ to $-28$~pp): at matched PSNR, QIM concentrates its
distortion into a large step ($\Delta\approx52$ here), which buys margin
against perturbations that do not scale, whereas DP-QIM's carriers are
ordinary natural values whose distance to the cell boundary is often small.

\subsection{Removal attack}
The UnMarker-style attack reduces DP-QIM to 0.97 ($\tau{=}2,j{=}0.5$) and 0.91
($\tau{=}1.5,j{=}1$) bit accuracy, 3 and 7~pp below matched QIM. Because
DP-QIM shows no histogram peaks, the attack's flagged bins mostly reflect image
content, and its jitter then acts as additive noise, the regime in which QIM's
larger margin wins. Undetectability thus does not by itself translate into
removal resistance. What it does deny the attacker is the ability to tell
watermarked from unwatermarked images (Table~\ref{tab:detect}), so a removal
attack cannot be applied selectively and must degrade all content it touches.

\subsection{Effect of position}
\label{sec:ablation}

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Gain (pp) of DP-QIM ($\epsilon{=}2$) over PSNR-matched QIM at three
DCT positions. Bold: 95\% CI excludes zero.}
\label{tab:ablation}
\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{\input{tables/ablation.tex}}
\end{table}

Table~\ref{tab:ablation} repeats the comparison at $(2,2)$ and $(4,3)$. The
blur and pure-scaling gains hold at every position ($+20$ to $+35$~pp), and the
noise and requantization costs persist. The downscaling gain depends on
position: it is largest at $(3,3)$, small at $(4,3)$, where downscaling
attenuates the carrier so strongly that DP-QIM's sign is itself lost, and
reverses at $(2,2)$, where attenuation is mild enough for QIM to survive. This
position dependence is why the baseline must be evaluated at the same position
as the proposed method; in an earlier version of our own pipeline the baseline
sat at a higher frequency than DP-QIM, which inflated the apparent gains.

%------------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

\textbf{When to use DP-QIM.} DP-QIM is preferable where an adversary should
not be able to tell which images are marked, or where marked images are likely
to be resized, filtered or tone-adjusted; QIM remains preferable where JPEG
recompression and noise dominate and detectability is irrelevant. The two
are complementary, which suggests hybrids that carry part of a payload with
each; we leave this to future work.

\textbf{Evaluation pitfalls.} Rebuilding our evaluation exposed errors that
we believe are easy to make: comparing methods at different DCT positions;
building the attacker's ``natural'' reference from the embedder's own samples,
which makes the defense look invisible by construction; computing per-image
KS statistics on 64 samples, whose null distribution already has mean
$\approx0.11$; fitting statistics on test images; and seeding payloads with
Python's per-process salted \texttt{hash()}. Each changed our conclusions.
The released protocol guards against all of them, and we recommend it for
future comparisons of quantization watermarks.

%------------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Data.} 44 crops from 15 photographs, all distributed with open
software; we could not run Kodak or DIV2K in our build environment. The
loaders accept local folders, and these benchmarks are the immediate next
step.
\item \textbf{Baselines.} We compare only with lattice QIM. Gain-invariant QIM
variants~\cite{PerezGonzalez2005rdm,Ourique2005angleqim,Li2007perceptualqim}
would likely close the scaling gap while keeping a lattice fingerprint, and
learned watermarks~\cite{Zhu2018hidden,Tancik2020stegastamp} use different
carriers; both comparisons are needed.
\item \textbf{Attacks and detectors.} Our UnMarker-style attack follows the
published description, not the authors' code, and we do not evaluate
regeneration attacks. Our detectors are histogram-based; rich-model or
CNN steganalyzers~\cite{Fridrich2012richmodels} may detect DP-QIM better.
\item \textbf{Capacity and fidelity.} One bit per block at a single position;
$M>1$ was numerically fragile. Because a moved carrier is replaced by a random
natural sample, DP-QIM's distortion is higher than necessary and its operating
range at 64~bits is 51 to 55~dB, whereas QIM reaches above 70~dB. Sampling the
replacement conditionally on the original magnitude could raise fidelity
without breaking Prop.~\ref{prop:ks}.
\end{itemize}

%------------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

Constraining a QIM-style watermark to preserve the natural coefficient
distribution makes it effectively invisible to histogram-based detection and,
for one-bit cells split at a zero median, invariant to amplitude scaling. On
real photographs at matched fidelity this yields large gains under blur,
downscaling and contrast reduction, at the cost of margin against JPEG,
additive noise and an UnMarker-style removal attack. Matching the natural
distribution is therefore a real lever for watermark security, but not a free
one, and it does not by itself defeat removal.
